title: "Building a Roster: Positional Value, the Cap, Free Agency, and the Draft"
subtitle: "How X's and O's turn into money: which players are worth paying, how a contract really hits the cap, where players come from, and why the same lineman is worth more to one team than another"
description: "How NFL rosters are built and paid for: positional value measured with contract data (what the market pays each position, why spending on a position barely predicts wins, and why quarterback play does); cap mechanics (cap hit, signing-bonus proration, guaranteed money, dead money, restructures, void years, the June 1 designation); acquisition (unrestricted and restricted free agents, the franchise and transition tags, compensatory picks, trades and the trade deadline, waivers); the draft (the rookie wage scale, the fifth-year option and the rookie-contract window, the Jimmy Johnson chart against a surplus-value curve built from nflverse contract data, Massey and Thaler's 'Loser's Curse'); scouting by position, the combine, pro days and RAS; scheme fit for linemen and corners; and roster rules (the 53, 48 game-day actives, practice-squad elevations, injured reserve and the emergency third quarterback). Team examples: the 2021 Rams, the Eagles' offensive line, the 49ers' mid-round linemen, and Brock Purdy's 2022-2024 rookie-contract window."
glossary:
  "Positional value": "How much a position, as opposed to a particular player, contributes to winning, and so how much a team should be willing to pay or draft for it. Quarterback is far ahead of everything else; edge rusher and wide receiver come next, then interior pass rushers, offensive tackles and cornerbacks; running back, off-ball linebacker, safety and tight end are near the bottom."
  "Cap hit": "The amount a player's contract counts against his team's salary cap in one league year: his base salary, the year's share of his signing bonus, and any roster, workout or incentive bonuses counted that year. It is an accounting number, not the cash he is paid that year."
  "Signing-bonus proration": "The cap rule that spreads a signing bonus evenly over the contract's years, up to five, even though the player is paid the money up front. A $50 million bonus on a five-year deal counts $10 million a year."
  "Guaranteed money": "Contract money a team must pay even if it releases the player. 'Fully guaranteed at signing' money is owed no matter what; other money is guaranteed only for injury, or becomes guaranteed on a later date if the player is still on the roster. Reported 'total guarantees' usually add the kinds together."
  "Dead money": "Cap charges for players no longer on the roster: when a team releases or trades a player, every year of his signing bonus not yet counted (and any guaranteed salary it still owes) hits the cap at once. It pays for no one on the field."
  "Void years": "Fake final years added to a contract that will cancel automatically before they are played. They exist only to spread a signing bonus over more years, which lowers today's cap hits; when the years void, the bonus not yet counted becomes dead money."
  "Unrestricted free agent": {def: "A player whose contract has expired and who has at least four accrued seasons (seasons with six or more games on full pay status). He may sign with any team, and his old team gets nothing back except, sometimes, a compensatory pick.", aliases: ["UFA"]}
  "Restricted free agent": {def: "A player whose contract has expired after exactly three accrued seasons. If his team offers him a qualifying one-year 'tender', he may negotiate with other teams, but his old team may match any offer sheet he signs or, depending on the tender, take a draft pick as compensation.", aliases: ["RFA"]}
  "Franchise tag": "A one-year contract a team may impose on one of its expiring players each year, priced at roughly the average of the five largest cap numbers at his position (or 120% of his previous salary, if higher). The non-exclusive tag lets other teams bid at the price of two first-round picks; the exclusive tag forbids talking to other teams at all."
  "Transition tag": "A cheaper cousin of the franchise tag, priced from the top ten salaries at the position: the player is held for one year, other teams may sign him to an offer sheet, and his team gets only the right to match, with no compensation if it doesn't."
  "Compensatory pick": "An extra draft pick, at the end of rounds 3 to 7, awarded to a team that lost more or better unrestricted free agents than it signed the year before. The league's formula weighs each player's new salary, playing time and honors; at most 32 are awarded a year."
  "Trade deadline": "The last day in a season on which NFL teams may trade players: since 2024, the Tuesday after Week 9. After it, rosters can change only through free agents, waivers and practice squads."
  "Waivers": "The system for releasing a player who has fewer than four accrued seasons (and, after the trade deadline, anyone): for about a day, every other team may claim him and take over his contract, with priority to the team with the worst record."
  "Rookie wage scale": "The fixed pay system for drafted rookies, introduced in the 2011 collective bargaining agreement: every draft slot carries a set four-year contract value, falling steeply from the first pick to the last, with little room to negotiate."
  "Rookie-contract window": "The years in which a team's good young player, above all a quarterback, is still on his cheap rookie deal. The gap between his pay and what a veteran of his quality costs is money the team can spend elsewhere, and the window closes when he signs his second contract."
  "Fifth-year option": "A team's right, written into every first-round rookie contract, to add a fifth season at a set price. It must be exercised after the player's third season; since the 2020 agreement the option year is fully guaranteed once exercised, and its price depends on his playing time and Pro Bowls."
  "Draft value chart": "A table that assigns every draft pick a number of points so that teams can price trades. The original, built for the Dallas Cowboys around 1991, is called the Jimmy Johnson chart; newer charts are built from what picks actually produce."
  "Surplus value": "What a player produces minus what he is paid. For a draft pick it is the on-field value the pick is expected to bring during the rookie contract, minus the rookie wage scale cost of that slot."
  "NFL Scouting Combine": {def: "The league's week-long scouting event for more than 300 invited draft prospects, held in Indianapolis each February and March: medical exams, interviews, body measurements and timed drills such as the 40-yard dash, vertical and broad jumps, bench press, three-cone drill and short shuttle.", aliases: ["Combine"]}
  "Pro day": "A workout held at a college campus in March and April for that school's draft prospects, attended by NFL scouts and coaches; players who skipped or could not finish the combine drills run them here, usually on their own turf and often with friendlier timing."
  "RAS": {def: "Relative Athletic Score: Kent Lee Platte's 0-to-10 summary of a prospect's measurements and drills, each converted to a percentile against every player measured at his position since 1987 and then combined. A 5 is average for the position, a 9 or above elite.", aliases: ["Relative Athletic Score"]}
  "Scheme fit": "How well a player's body type and skills match what a particular scheme asks of his position, which makes the same player worth more to one team than another: a lighter, quick guard for a wide-zone team, a bigger drive blocker for a gap team; a heavy two-gap nose for some 3-4 defenses, a quick one-gap 3-technique for an attacking four-man front; a long press corner or a quick off-coverage corner."
  "Practice squad elevation": "Moving a practice-squad player up to the game-day roster for one game, after which he returns to the practice squad without being exposed to waivers. A team may elevate two players a game, and each player at most three times a season."
  "Injured reserve": {def: "The list for injured players who are removed from the 53-man roster, freeing their spots. A player placed on it during the season must sit out at least four games; a team may bring back a limited number (eight a season) and the rest are out for the year.", aliases: ["IR"]}
  "Emergency third quarterback": "Since 2023, a third quarterback on the 53-man roster who may dress for a game without counting against the game-day active limit, and enter only if both of the team's other quarterbacks are injured or ejected."

## The problem: 53 players, one budget, and a draft

An NFL general manager has three constraints that no fantasy league or Madden franchise mode quite
captures.

**The cap is hard.** Every team gets the same [salary cap](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-salary-cap)
for each **league year**, the NFL's business year, which starts in mid-March. It is set from a share of
league revenue: $279.2 million for 2025 and $301.2 million for 2026, the first time it has passed $300
million.[^cap]
Unlike baseball or the NBA, there is no luxury tax that lets a rich owner pay his way over it. A dollar
spent on one player is a dollar that can't be spent on anyone else, so every contract is a decision
about the whole roster.

**The roster is big and the game is specialized.** A team carries 53 players, dresses 48 on game day, and
needs starters at about 25 different jobs once you count the kicker, punter and long snapper. A left
tackle can't play cornerback. So the budget can't simply follow "buy the best players"; it has to buy a
*team*, with a backup at every spot the season will expose.

**Most talent arrives through a draft you don't control.** The worst teams pick first, and rookies are
paid on a fixed scale. That makes the draft the cheapest source of good players, and it means a team's
cost of talent depends on *when* it acquired a player as much as on how good he is.

Put those together and the GM's real question isn't "who is good?" It is "**where does the next dollar,
or the next pick, buy the most winning?**" The rest of this chapter is the toolkit for answering it.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the salary cap"}
The cap is a deal between the owners and the players' union, renewed in each **collective bargaining
agreement** (the current one, signed in 2020, runs through the 2030 season). The players get a fixed share of
league revenue, at least 48 percent, paid out through the cap and benefits; the owners get cost
certainty and a league in which a small-market team can afford the same roster as a big-market one.[^cba]
The trade-off is the one this chapter keeps returning to: under a hard cap, overpaying anyone is never
free, because someone else on the roster pays for it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden's franchise mode, cutting an expensive veteran usually frees his whole salary. In the NFL, a
release can *cost* cap space this year, because of the bonus money already paid (the dead money section
below shows why). And no real GM can trade three backups for a star the way the game's AI often accepts:
picks and players are priced by charts every front office knows.
:::

That chart is [**positional value**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-positional-value) as the market

22\.4% of the cap for a top-ten deal. Then come the

**Quarterback touches every snap.** He decides where the ball goes on every pass and many runs, and
[Expected Points](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd) showed that passing
plays carry more value per snap than runs and swing far more widely. A position that controls the
highest-leverage action on every play is worth more than one that matters on a third of them.

**The premium group decides the passing game.** An [edge rusher](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-edge-rusher)
who wins one-on-one ends drives with sacks
and hurried throws; the offensive tackles are the men assigned to stop him. The old idea was that only the
left tackle mattered, because he guards a right-handed quarterback's blind side, the side he can't see.
The market no longer believes it: 4 of the ten richest tackle contracts belong to
right tackles. A receiver who wins against man coverage gives the

help elsewhere. Every one of those players wins or loses a matchup on most passing downs, and they are
scarce: you can't develop a 6-foot-5, 265-pound man who runs a 4.5 forty from the seventh round.

**The bottom group is either replaceable or rarely decisive.** Running back is the classic case. Most of
a run's yards are created by the blockers and the scheme before the back touches the ball (13-02's
rush-yards-over-expected showed how little separates most backs once you account for the blocking),
backs wear down quickly, and the college game produces good ones every year. Off-ball linebackers and
safeties matter, but they win fewer one-on-one matchups that decide plays, and they are easier to find.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Running backs don't matter." Positional value is about *price*, not about whether a position matters.
Saquon Barkley ran for 2,005 yards for the 2024 Eagles and was central to a Super Bowl run (the

is narrower: the gap between a great back and a decent one is smaller than the gap between their
salaries, so the money usually buys more at another position. The Eagles could pay Barkley because they
had built cheaply elsewhere, which is the real lesson of positional value.
:::

## How a contract really hits the cap

A headline says "five years, $150 million." Almost none of that number tells you what the team will
actually carry on its cap in a given year, or what it would cost to get out of the deal. Four ideas do.

**The [cap hit](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cap-hit)** is what a contract counts against the cap
in one league year: the player's base salary for that year, plus the year's share of his signing bonus,
plus any roster, workout or incentive bonuses counted that year. It is an accounting number, not the cash
paid. The broadcast graphic shows it because it's the number that limits the team.

**[Signing-bonus proration](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-signing-bonus-proration)** is the rule that
creates the gap between cash and cap. A signing bonus is paid to the player up front (often within
months), but for cap purposes it is spread evenly over the years of the contract, up to a maximum of
five. That is why teams love signing bonuses: the player gets the cash now, and the team spreads the cap
cost into future years, when the cap will usually be higher, so the same fixed charge is a smaller share
of it.

**[Guaranteed money](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-guaranteed-money)** is money the team must pay
even if it releases the player. It comes in flavors: *fully guaranteed at signing* (owed no matter
what), *injury-only* (owed if he is cut while hurt), and money that **vests**, becoming fully guaranteed
on a set date, often a few days into the new league year, if he is still on the roster. Agents and
reporters often quote the total of all of these, which is why "total guarantees" in a headline can be far
larger than what the player is truly certain to receive.

**[Dead money](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dead-money)** is the bill for leaving early. If a team
releases or trades a player, every year of signing-bonus proration not yet counted lands on the cap at
once, along with any guaranteed salary still owed. That money pays for nobody on the field.

Read the top panel first. The player is paid $55 million in cash in year 1 (the $50 million bonus plus

contract is built around a large signing bonus: it front-loads the player's money and back-loads the
team's cap cost. Typically the bonus plus the first year or two of salary are fully guaranteed at signing,
here $75 million, and the later years are not, which is what makes them "team-friendly": the team can
walk away from them.

### Restructures and void years: borrowing from the future

The middle panel is the most common move in the cap world, the **restructure**. A team needs cap space this
year, so it asks a player it plans to keep to turn most of this year's base salary into a signing bonus.
The player loses nothing: he gets the same money sooner, it becomes guaranteed, and the extra dead money it
creates makes him harder to cut, which is job security. The team spreads the new bonus over the remaining
years and cuts this year's cap hit sharply. The catch is that later cap hits rise by the same total, so a
restructure is borrowing, not saving.

[**Void years**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-void-years) stretch the loan. They are fake final
years added to the contract that cancel automatically before anyone plays them. Their only purpose is to
give the bonus more years to spread across, which lowers each year's charge. When they cancel, whatever
proration was assigned to them becomes dead money all at once. The league tolerates them because they
move cap charges without erasing any: every bonus dollar still counts against some year's cap. Tom Brady's last Tampa Bay contracts were
the famous example: after he retired in February 2023, the Buccaneers carried about $35 million of dead
money for a quarterback who was no longer playing.[^brady]

### Cutting a player, and why June 1 matters

The bottom panel is the release. After year 2, the player's last three years carry $30 million of
proration that hasn't been counted. Cut him in March and all $30 million is dead money this year, so the
release saves only $5 million of cap (his $35 million cap hit minus $30 million of dead money) even
though it saves $25 million of cash. That is why you hear "they can't afford to cut him": sometimes cutting
a player costs nearly as much cap space as keeping him.

The **June 1 rule** softens it. If a player is released after June 1, or released earlier with a post-June
1 designation (each team gets two a year), only the current year's proration counts this year and the
rest moves to next year. The team gets more room now and pays the remainder later. The catch is timing: a
designated player's full cap hit stays on the books until June 2, so the designation doesn't help a team
that needs room in March, when free agency opens.

Two more rules shape how much room a team really has. From the start of the league year until the season,
only a team's 51 largest contracts count in full (the **top-51 rule**), so cutting a player saves his cap hit
minus the cost of the minimum-salary player who moves up into the top 51. And unused cap space can be
**carried over** into the next league year, which is why some teams deliberately "bank" room.[^cbacap]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Denver Broncos, 2024"}
**The move:** Denver released quarterback Russell Wilson two years after trading for him and signing him to
a five-year, $245 million extension. The release created **$85 million of dead money**, the largest
amount in league history at the time.[^wilson]

**Why March:** on the fifth day of the 2024 league year, another $37 million of Wilson's future salary would
have turned from guaranteed-for-injury into fully guaranteed. Cutting him on the first day of the league year
kept that money off the bill. **Why two years:** the release carried a post-June 1 designation, so the charge
was split across two league years, and Denver chose to take the larger part, a record $53 million, on the 2024
cap and $32 million on 2025.

**What to notice:** why a team would accept that. Wilson's remaining guaranteed money had to be paid either
way, so keeping him cost the same money plus a roster spot for a player the coaches had benched. Dead money
is a **sunk cost**: it is spent whatever you do next, and good front offices decide on what each choice costs
*from here*. Denver spent 2024 with a rookie quarterback, Bo Nix, on a rookie contract, and made the
playoffs; in 2025 it went 14–3 and earned the AFC's top seed while still carrying the second half of the
Wilson charge. A painful cap year is survivable when the replacement is cheap.
:::

### Free agency: unrestricted and restricted

When a contract expires, what happens depends on the player's **accrued seasons**, the seasons in which he
spent at least six regular-season games on full pay status (on the active roster, inactive, or on injured
reserve).

- An **[unrestricted free agent](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-unrestricted-free-agent)** (**UFA**) has
  four or more accrued seasons. He may sign with anyone, and his old team gets nothing back except
  possibly a compensatory pick a year later (explained below). This is the market most fans picture: the first days of the
  league year in March, when the best players sign big deals, usually agreed during a two-day negotiating
  window just before it that broadcasters call "legal tampering".
- A **[restricted free agent](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-restricted-free-agent)** (**RFA**) has
  exactly three. His team can offer him a one-year **tender** at one of several set prices. He may then
  sign an **offer sheet** with another team, but his old team can match it; if it doesn't, it receives a
  draft pick whose round depends on the tender. Offer sheets are rare, because teams don't like giving up
  picks to pry a player loose. (With fewer than three seasons, a player can be kept for a minimum salary
  and can't negotiate elsewhere at all.)

**Why free agency exists:** it is the players' half of the 1993 bargain that also created the cap (see
[11-02](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd)). **What it costs teams:** free agents are usually
paid for what they did on their last team, at the peak of their market, and a bidding war means the team
that "wins" is the one that valued him most, often too much. Analysts call that the **winner's curse**,
and it's why patient teams treat free agency as a way to fill specific holes rather than to build a
roster.

### The franchise and transition tags

What if the player is a star and the team can't agree on a long-term deal? It can **tag** him.

The **[franchise tag](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-franchise-tag)** is a one-year contract that a team
may impose on one expiring player a year. Its price is set by formula: roughly the average of the five
largest cap numbers at his position, or 120 percent of his previous salary, whichever is higher. The
usual **non-exclusive** tag lets other teams bid, but his team may match, and if it doesn't it receives two
first-round picks, a price that almost always ends the conversation; the pricier **exclusive** tag forbids
talking to other teams at all.

The **[transition tag](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-transition-tag)** is the cheaper version, priced
from the top ten salaries at the position. Other teams can sign the player to an offer sheet, and his team
gets only the right to match, with no compensation if it lets him go.[^tags]

**Why tags exist:** to let a team keep a great player for one more season while the two sides keep
negotiating; a tagged player and his team have until mid-July to agree on a long-term deal, or he plays
the year on the tag. **What a tag costs:** a full year of top-of-market salary, fully guaranteed, with no
cap-friendly bonus structure, and a player who usually feels he has been denied his long-term security.
Tagging the same player again costs more each time. Washington tagged quarterback Kirk Cousins in 2016 and
again in 2017, then let him walk; Minnesota signed him in 2018 to a three-year, $84 million contract that
was **fully guaranteed**, the first multi-year fully guaranteed deal for a quarterback and a direct result
of the leverage two tags had given him.[^cousins]

Because the tag is priced by position, it is also where scheme meets money. In 2014 the Saints tagged Jimmy
Graham as a tight end, at about $7 million; Graham argued that he lined up in the slot or out wide so often
that he was really a receiver, whose tag was about $12.3 million. An arbitrator ruled that a tight end
detached from the line in the slot is still doing a tight end's job, and Graham lost.[^graham] The label on
a player's role is worth millions, which is the idea [Scheme and Fantasy](14-02-scheme-and-fantasy.qmd)
picks up.

### Compensatory picks

A team that loses more good free agents than it signs gets a consolation prize. The
**[compensatory pick](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-compensatory-pick)** formula looks at every
unrestricted free agent who left or arrived the previous year, ranks each by his new contract's average
salary, playing time and honors, and awards up to 32 extra picks league-wide, at the end of rounds 3
through 7, at most four per team. Since 2017 the picks can be traded.[^comp] The idea is to repay a team for
talent it developed and then lost on the open market.

**Why it matters for strategy:** the formula nets the two lists. Every qualifying free agent a team
*signs* cancels out one it *lost*, roughly matched by contract size. Only players whose contracts ran out
count; a player who was released doesn't count on either side. So a team can choose to let its own free
agents walk, sign only veterans other teams have cut, and collect the picks.[^compnet] The Baltimore Ravens are the model: they have received more
compensatory picks than any other franchise since the system began in 1994, and their roster is built
on letting expensive veterans walk at the right time.[^ravens]

### Trades and the trade deadline

A trade moves a contract, not just a player. The acquiring team takes over his remaining salary and cap
hits; the trading team keeps any signing-bonus proration it has not yet counted, as dead money. When a
broadcast says a team "ate" money to make a deal work, that is what it means: it took a dead-money charge
so that the other team would take the player. Trades also cluster around the
new league year in March, because a trade agreed after the season can't be processed until then, and
because that is when next year's cap numbers start to count.

The **[trade deadline](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trade-deadline)** is the last day of the season on
which trades are allowed: since 2024, the Tuesday after Week 9.[^deadline]
After it, a contender can add only free agents, waiver claims and its own practice squad. So contenders
use the deadline to **rent** a veteran for a playoff run, paying with future picks, and sellers turn a
player who won't be part of their next good team into a pick that might be.

### Waivers

When a team releases a player with fewer than four accrued seasons (and, after the trade deadline, any
player, so that a contender can't sign a veteran whom a rival releases to get around the deadline), he goes on **[waivers](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-waivers)**: for about a day, every other
team may claim him and take over his contract as it stands. If several teams claim him, the one with the
worst record wins. A player nobody claims becomes a free agent and can choose his next team. Waivers
matter most on cut-down day in late August, when hundreds of players are released at once and every front
office combs the list for someone better than its own 53rd man.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams, 2021"}
**The build:** the Rams of 2021 are the boldest trade-built champion of the cap era. In March they made official the
trade for quarterback Matthew Stafford, sending Detroit Jared Goff, a 2021 third-round pick and their first-round
picks in 2022 and 2023. They already had cornerback Jalen Ramsey, acquired in 2019 for two first-round picks and a
fourth. At the trade deadline they added edge rusher Von Miller for a 2022 second- and third-round
pick. A week later Cleveland released Odell Beckham Jr. Because the deadline had passed, even a veteran had to
go through waivers; nobody claimed his contract, which made him a free agent free to pick his team, and he
chose Los Angeles.[^rams] On February 13, 2022, the Rams beat Cincinnati 23–20 in Super Bowl
LVI: Beckham caught the game's first touchdown, Miller had two sacks, and Stafford threw three touchdown passes.

**What to notice:** the currency. The Rams paid in *future* draft picks, which a team with a short window values
least, and spent them on premium positions (a quarterback, a cornerback, an edge rusher) rather than on depth.
The bill came later: the Rams did not make a
first-round pick in any draft from 2017
through 2023 (their first after Jared Goff in 2016 was Jared Verse, 19th overall in 2024), and went 5–12 in 2022 with an injured, expensive roster. They drafted their way back (Puka Nacua was
a 2023 fifth-round pick) and were back in the playoffs in 2023. A trade-built roster wins a window; it doesn't
build a pipeline.
:::

## The draft: the cheapest good players in football

### The rookie wage scale and the fifth-year option

Before 2011, top draft picks negotiated like free agents, and the price had run away: the 2010 first overall
pick, quarterback Sam Bradford, signed a six-year deal worth up to $78 million with $50 million guaranteed
before playing a down, more than many proven veteran quarterbacks earned. The 2011 collective bargaining
agreement ended that with the **[rookie wage scale](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rookie-wage-scale)**.
Every draft slot now carries a set four-year contract value, falling steeply from the first pick to the last,
with little left to negotiate. Drafted players cannot sign an extension until after their third regular
season.[^rookie]

First-round picks come with one extra year of team control. The
**[fifth-year option](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fifth-year-option)** lets the team add a fifth
season at a set price, decided after the player's third season (by early May). Since the 2020 agreement
the option is fully guaranteed once exercised, and its price depends on how much the player has played and
whether he made Pro Bowls, so teams now decline it for players they aren't sure of.

Together these rules create the **[rookie-contract window](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rookie-contract-window)**:
the years in which a good young player is paid far less than a veteran of his quality. For a star it usually
lasts three seasons, not four or five, because the first moment an extension is allowed (after year 3) is
also the moment his team rushes to lock him up before his price climbs further. For most positions the
window is a nice bonus. For a quarterback it is the most valuable asset in the sport, as
@fig-qb-price-play showed, and teams with a young starter build their entire cap plan around it.

### Draft value charts: what is a pick worth?

To trade picks, teams need a common price list. The original
**[draft value chart](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-draft-value-chart)** was built for the Dallas
Cowboys in the early 1990s, under head coach Jimmy Johnson, from past trades and judgment: at Johnson's
request, Cowboys vice president Mike McCoy drew it up before the club's run of draft-day trades in
1991.[^jjchart]
The **Jimmy Johnson chart** gives the first pick 3,000 points, the 16th 1,000, the 32nd 590, the 64th 270
and the 100th 100. Teams still use it or close cousins, and a trade that "balances on the chart" is still
how deals get done. (Separately, each team ranks the prospects themselves on its **draft board**, its own
ordered list of players; the chart prices the slots, the board decides whom to take in them.)

But the chart describes what teams *pay* for picks, not what the picks *produce*. In 2005 two behavioral
economists, Cade Massey and Richard Thaler (Thaler later won a Nobel prize for work on how people make
predictable mistakes), asked whether the prices were right. They measured each pick's
**[surplus value](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-surplus-value)**: what a player produces minus what he
is paid. Their answer, published as "The Loser's Curse," was that teams badly overvalue the top of the draft.
A top pick is more likely to become a star, but he is also paid far more, and teams are overconfident in
their ability to tell the stars apart. By surplus value, they found, picks *gained* value through the first
round, because a pick's cost fell faster down the round than the production teams could expect from it, and
the best value in the draft sat in the second round.[^mt]
The curse of the title: the worst team earns the first pick, and the first pick is overpriced.

Their data came from before the rookie wage scale, when top picks were far more expensive. We can redo the
idea for the current era with contract data. For every player drafted from 2011 to 2020, take what the market
paid him on his **next** contract (as a share of the cap) as the measure of what he turned out to be worth, and
take his rookie salary as what he cost. Surplus is the difference. Why the next contract? Because when a
rookie deal ends, 32 front offices that watched him for four years bid on him, and the price they settle on is
the best available summary of how good he was; a player nobody would pay counts as zero. The two halves come
from different years on purpose: value from the 2011–2020 classes, because later classes haven't all reached
a second contract yet, and cost from 2021–2025 rookie deals, because those are today's prices.

the chart says, and a team trading *up* is usually paying more.

excellent and then hurt, and it credits players paid on reputation. And the top of the curve rests on very
few players, mostly quarterbacks: 7 of the ten first overall picks from 2011 to 2020.

quarterback on a rookie deal is worth more than either chart's price, so a team convinced it has found one
can rationally pay almost anything; that is why the biggest trade-ups are for quarterbacks. Everywhere else,
and above all in trades that bundle several picks or future first-rounders, the choice of chart decides
who won. The catch in the quarterback exception is that the conviction is often wrong, as the next film

### The combine and pro days

Film is graded through the fall. In February and March come the measurements. The
**[NFL Scouting Combine](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nfl-scouting-combine)** brings more than 300 invited
prospects (319 in 2026) to Indianapolis, where it has been held since 1987, for a week of medical exams,
interviews with teams, body measurements (height, weight, arm length, hand size) and timed drills.[^combine]
Each drill stands in for a football trait:

- **40-yard dash**, with a **10-yard split**: long speed for receivers, backs and corners; the split, the
  first ten yards, is the closest number to a lineman's or edge rusher's burst off the snap.
- **Vertical and broad jump**: lower-body explosiveness.
- **Bench press** (reps of 225 pounds): upper-body strength endurance, mostly for linemen.
- **Three-cone drill** and **20-yard short shuttle**: change of direction, the ability to stop, bend and
  restart, which matters for edge rushers turning the corner and corners mirroring routes.

A **[pro day](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pro-day)** is the campus version, held in March and April
for a school's prospects with NFL scouts and coaches watching. Players who skipped drills at the combine
run them here, usually on their own familiar turf and often with friendlier timing, so experienced
evaluators treat pro-day numbers as slightly optimistic.

### RAS: putting the numbers on one scale

A 4.6 forty is slow for a cornerback and astonishing for a 300-pound tackle, so raw numbers can't be
compared across positions. **[RAS](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-ras)**, the **Relative Athletic Score**
created by the analyst Kent Lee Platte, solves that by converting each measurement into a percentile among
every player measured at the same position since 1987, then combining them into one score from 0 to 10. A 5
is average for the position; 8 is very good; 9 and above is elite.[^ras]

## Scheme fit: the same player, different value

Here is where X's and O's come back. **[Scheme fit](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scheme-fit)** is how
well a player's body and skills match what a particular scheme asks of his position. Because schemes ask
different things, the same prospect can be a first-round talent on one board and a fourth-rounder on another,
and a smart team shops where its scheme makes it the only serious buyer.

### Defensive line: two-gap nose or one-gap 3-technique

The same split runs through the defensive front. In a two-gap defense, often a
[3-4](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-4) with a [nose tackle](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nose-tackle)
head-up on the center, the lineman's job is to strike the blocker, control him, and be ready to shed into
*either* gap beside him ([two-gap](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-gap) play). In a one-gap attacking
front, the [3-technique](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-technique) on the guard's outside shoulder
owns a single gap and shoots into it at the snap ([one-gap](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-one-gap) play).
[DL Techniques and Gap Control](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)

Pure two-gap 3-4 defenses are rare now, but the heavy nose came back another way: the
[tite front](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tite-front)
([Odd and Hybrid Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd)) puts a nose
on the center and two linemen on the tackles' inside shoulders to wall off inside runs, and it needs a big
man in the middle again. The Eagles drafted both archetypes in back-to-back first rounds: Jordan Davis
(No. 13 in 2022, 341 pounds at the combine), a nose, and Jalen Carter (No. 9 in 2023, 314 pounds), a
penetrating 3-technique.[^phidl]

The edge has the same split. A 4-3 defensive end plays with his hand in the dirt and must hold up against
tackles in the run game, so teams like him heavier, around 255–280 pounds; a 3-4 outside linebacker stands
up, rushes from wider and sometimes drops into coverage, so he can be lighter and quicker, around 240–260.
But defenses played their base personnel on only about 30 percent of snaps in 2025, and spent the rest with
five or more defensive backs,[^base] so whatever the base front is called, the live split today is less
"4-3 end or 3-4 linebacker" than "run-down edge or pass-rush specialist".

### Cornerbacks: press or off

Cornerbacks split by technique, not by man versus zone. A team whose corners play
[press](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-press), jamming the receiver at the line, wants long, physical
corners with the hips to turn and the long speed to run with a go route, whether they then play man or
bail into a zone. Pete Carroll's Seattle teams of the 2010s, the league's signature press Cover 3 defense
([Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)), drafted outside corners with
long arms and nearly all of them six feet or taller.[^seacb] A team whose corners play
[off coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-off-coverage), with a cushion and their eyes in the
backfield, can live with shorter corners who read the play and break on the ball quickly. The clearest case
is the Cover 2 [squat corner](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-squat-corner), who sits about five to seven
yards off, keeps the flat and hands the deep ball to a safety: Ronde Barber, listed at 5 feet 10, played that
role in Tampa Bay's [Tampa 2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tampa-2) on his way to the Hall of Fame.[^barber]

**Game-day actives.** A team may dress 48 of its 53, provided at least eight are offensive linemen
(otherwise 47); the rest are declared inactive about 90 minutes before kickoff. Who sits is a weekly game-plan
decision. A team facing a run-heavy opponent might dress a fifth defensive tackle instead of a sixth
receiver, and the inactive list on Sunday morning is one of the best free clues to the plan.

**The practice squad.** Each team keeps 16 players on its practice squad (plus one exemption for an
international player). They practice with the team but are not on the 53, and any other team may sign one to its 53 at any time.
A **[practice squad elevation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-practice-squad-elevation)** moves one of them
up for a single game: a team may elevate two a game, each player at most three times a season, and he reverts
to the practice squad afterward without going through waivers. That is how a team covers a Saturday injury
without cutting anyone, and it's why a "practice squad" kicker can make a game-winning field goal.[^ps]

**[Injured reserve](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-injured-reserve)** (**IR**) takes an injured player off the
53 so his spot can be filled. During the season a player placed on IR must sit out at least four games, and a
team can bring back a limited number of players a year (eight); everyone else stays out for the season. The
rule creates a real decision: put a player with a six-week injury on IR, freeing his spot for a healthy body, or
keep him on the 53 and play a man short for a month and a half.

**The [emergency third quarterback](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-emergency-third-quarterback).** Since 2023
a team may dress a third quarterback from its 53 without counting him among the 48, and he may enter only if both
of the other quarterbacks are injured or ejected. The rule was a direct answer to the 2022 NFC Championship
Game, in which San Francisco lost its starter to an elbow injury and then its backup to a concussion; with a
running back as the only other option, the injured starter went back in, barely able to throw.[^eqb]

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: the cap check"}
Pick one team before its game (Over the Cap and Spotrac have free team pages) and do a five-minute cap check.
On an Over the Cap team page, the cap hit is the **Cap Number** column, and a **Dead Money & Cap Savings**
section shows, for each player, what cutting him would leave as dead money and save, with separate
"Cut (pre-June 1)" and "Cut (post-June 1)" views. Use the pre-June 1 view for March decisions.

**Before kickoff**

- **Find the five biggest cap hits.** Are they at premium positions (QB, edge, receiver, interior pass
  rusher, tackle, corner)? A top-five hit at running back, linebacker or safety is a team paying for a player, not a
  position.
- **Find the dead money.** A large number means a recent mistake or a recent release; it tells you
  which era of the roster the team is paying for.
- **Is the quarterback on a rookie contract?** If so, look for the team spending the savings: expensive
  veterans elsewhere, a deadline trade. If not, look for bargains and late-round starters around him.
- **Check the inactives** (posted 90 minutes before kickoff) and any **practice-squad elevations**
  announced the day before. They tell you the game plan's priorities and who is hurt.

**During the game**

- When a veteran with a big cap hit plays poorly, ask the cap question: what would releasing him save,
  and how much dead money would it leave? A small dead-money figure next to a big cap hit is a player
  likely to be released or asked to take a pay cut in March.
- When a young player on a rookie deal plays well at a premium position, you are watching his team's cap
  plan for the next three years.

**The prediction:** before the season ends, name the one contract the team will **restructure** (a star it
plans to keep, with a large base salary next year) and the one it will **cut** (an older player at a

**The team must clear $14 million before free agency opens in March. Which moves clear it most cheaply? On
the radio, one caller says to cut the quarterback, the single biggest saving on the board; another says to
cut the 32-year-old left tackle. Why are both wrong?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Release the running back and the linebacker ($20 million saved); don't touch the quarterback or the left
tackle.**

Start with the cuts that are cheap *and* sensible. The running back saves $12 million against $2 million of dead
money, at the position the market values least, at an age when backs decline fast. That isn't quite enough, so add
the linebacker ($8 million saved, $1 million dead), another low-value position and another player past 30:
$20 million cleared. (The top-51 rule trims that a little, since two minimum-salary players move up into the 51
that count, but it still clears 14.) Both are pre-June 1 releases on purpose: a post-June 1 designation would leave
their cap hits on the books until June 2, after free agency has opened.

The other lever is a restructure. Turning $30 million of the quarterback's $40 million base salary into a bonus
spread over his three remaining seasons counts $10 million a year, so next year's hit falls by $20 million. The cost
is the future: his next two cap hits each rise by $10 million, and his dead money grows by $20 million on top of
the $36 million already there, which makes him almost impossible to cut. Fine for a quarterback the team is sure
of; a trap for one it isn't. Most teams would make the two cheap cuts and save the restructure for when they need
room to *add* someone.

Now the callers. Cutting the quarterback saves $16 million but leaves $36 million of dead money and no starter,
and replacing a starting quarterback costs far more than $16 million. The left tackle is the subtler trap: $15
million saved, but tackle is a premium position, replacements are expensive, and the quarterback needs protecting.
If he is still good, the hole costs more to fill than the cut saves. The edge rusher and cornerback are young
premium players with heavy dead money, extension candidates rather than cuts; the receiver, at 30, is more likely
to be asked to take a pay cut.
:::

**It is outside zone, and the team takes Prospect B.** Every lineman's first step is sideways and to the
right, with the back aiming wide and cutting up: that is

That is a race, and B's quickness (a 4.45 short shuttle is excellent for a guard) and film ("quick to reach and
climb") are exactly the traits it rewards.

The cost is in pass protection. B gives ground to big bull rushers, and the team will have to cover for it:
help from the center on obvious passing downs, a quicker passing game, and play-action and boots that move the
launch point away from the defensive tackle. A wide-zone team can live with that because its run game and its
play-action both ask him to move, not to stand still and absorb a 330-pound man head-on.

Prospect A is the better *gap* lineman: heavy, long, with a stout anchor, and able to move a defender off his
spot on a down block, the power-team skill. On a gap team's board he may be the higher-rated player, and on
this team's board he is a worse fit who would spend his first year trying to win races he isn't built for.
That's scheme fit: the same pick, two right answers, depending on what the team runs. It also explains why a
wide-zone team can often draft B a round later than his talent suggests. Fewer teams are shopping for him.

## Takeaways

- **Positional value is real, but price is not value.** The market pays quarterbacks most by far, then edge
  rushers and receivers, then interior pass rushers, corners and tackles. Yet a team's share of spending on any position barely predicts
  winning (r near zero, 2014–2025), while quarterback *play* predicts it strongly (r about 0.7). Value comes from
  getting play above your price.
- **A contract is a cap schedule, not a number.** Signing bonuses are paid up front but prorated over up to five
  years; restructures and void years borrow cap space from the future; releasing a player accelerates his
  remaining proration as dead money, which is why cutting a star can save almost nothing.
- **Every acquisition route has a currency.** Free agency costs cap space at peak prices; tags buy one year at a
  top-of-market price; trades cost picks and move contracts; compensatory picks reward letting players go;
  waivers and the practice squad are how teams find the 53rd man.
- **The draft is the cheapest source of good players, and the Johnson chart overprices the top.** Surplus value
  (production minus rookie cost) falls far more gently than the chart, so trading down usually buys value and
  trading up usually pays a premium, except, sometimes, for a franchise quarterback.
- **The rookie-contract window is the biggest edge in roster building.** A star quarterback on a rookie deal, like
  Purdy in 2022–2024, frees a fifth or more of the cap to spend on everyone else.
- **Scheme decides who is worth drafting.** Wide-zone and gap teams want different linemen, two-gap and one-gap
  fronts want different tackles, press and off teams want different corners. RAS and the combine filter for
  athleticism; film and fit decide the pick.
